public_rationale: The checkable firm part is his statement, presented as fact, that 'you can't measure the cost of an LLM-driven task or its return on investment.' Before the post, researchers were publishing dollar costs per task for LLM systems. A March 2026 survey reports costs falling from $4,500 per task (o3) to $12 per task (GPT-5.2) on the ARC-AGI benchmark. So the cost of an LLM-driven task could be and was measured. The other parts are judgments without measures and are not scored. On profitability the evidence is split: Anthropic reported an operating profit of $974 million in Q2 2026, but a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of 2026. The grade rests only on the measurement part.
limitations: He may have meant that enterprises cannot easily track per-task cost or ROI under flat-rate subscriptions. That narrower point is not tested here.
The decisive item is a preprint about benchmark tasks, not commercial workloads.
Two parts of the sentence are left unscored.

statement.excerpt: Its services cost too much to run, its progenitors have no path to profitability, and no amount of rigged benchmarks and anecdotal examples of theoretical engineering teams that are “10x’d” can make up for the fact that you can’t measure the cost of an LLM-driven task or its return on investment.

from_speaker: Its services cost too much to run
its progenitors have no path to profitability
you can't measure the cost of an LLM-driven task or its return on investment
our_interpretation: The sentence has three parts. 'Cost too much to run' is a judgment with no threshold. 'No path to profitability' is a judgment about future prospects with no measure of profit, so it is weighed as context rather than scored on its own.

The checkable firm part is that the cost of an LLM-driven task cannot be measured. He presents it as a fact. Plain reading: there is no way to put a dollar cost on an individual task done with an LLM. Published, reproducible per-task dollar cost figures for LLM systems would contradict it.

He joins cost and ROI with 'or': you can't measure 'the cost ... or its return on investment.' Showing that per-task cost is routinely measured is enough to contradict that part, whatever one thinks of ROI measurement.
He describes a present state without naming a period. I use 2026-01-01 to the post date, the period public evidence could report on just before the post.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence that, at the time of the post, no method existed to state the dollar cost of an LLM-driven task: for example, providers and researchers did not or could not report per-task costs.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Dated public evidence from before the post in which researchers or providers report the dollar cost per task of LLM systems.
